compare_blocks.body:
The pricing, store meeting and dinner examples are fictional. They illustrate ways of using information or weighing a choice. Either person can use any of the approaches.

### ENTJ and ESFJ: pricing and the gift bundle

In this fictional review, both people compare the same three price tiers and gift options using the same costs and customer feedback. One consideration is whether each option meets an agreed margin threshold. Another is what customers get for the price and how easily staff can explain the offer. Either person can weigh both.

A price can meet the margin target while being hard to explain. An offer that customers appreciate can still cost more than the business can sustain. The fictional review illustrates the need to check both consequences before choosing.

Give both reviewers the financial assumptions and the staff feedback. Have each explain the basis for the numbers and what customers will hear. Allocate the work by access to information, experience and responsibility.

Write down what a customer might ask at each tier and what a staff member could say in response. Later, review sales, returns and repeat purchases together. Two fictional weeks of figures are not enough to establish a trend.

### ENTJ and ESFJ: a store manager objects to the price

In this fictional meeting, a manager says the product will not sell at the announced price. With the same store records, both reviewers can check what happened at comparable prices and look for a pattern that might explain the objection. Neither reaction establishes a type.

A store-level observation may reveal a problem that an aggregate figure hides. It may also reflect conditions unique to that store. The question is what evidence would support a change and where that change would apply.

The team can distinguish the evidence for changing a price from the consequences of changing the launch date. Record what is verified, what still needs checking and which choices remain open.

### ENTJ and ESFJ: twelve people for dinner on Saturday

(Fictional scene) Twelve people at home on Saturday, three of them children, one elder who does not eat spicy food. One person produces a timetable: when to shop, how many dishes, who washes up, with six o'clock fixed; the other makes calls one by one: who avoids what, who is bringing whom, whether the hard chair will do for the elder.

The two arrangements guard against different risks. The timetable guards against the day going sideways: not enough food, everyone arrived with nothing on the stove, the kitchen jammed; the calls guard against someone unable to eat, short of a seat, or placed where they cannot settle. Both risks are real, and either person can think of either one first.

The costs are plain: the timetable alone gets the food right and may leave people uncomfortable; the calls alone can reach Friday with no menu. The workable version runs both lines with a deadline each: numbers and dietary needs settled by Thursday, menu and seating by Friday. Who owns which line depends on who is at home that day and who knows these relatives better, not on type.

Either host can check dietary needs, revise the menu or prepare a schedule. In this fictional example, the hosts can compare the risks they each noticed and decide what still needs checking. The order of those checks does not identify either type.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
The most common misread is forcefulness. Both may settle a decision in a meeting and chase progress; volume and the speed of a call prove neither T nor N, and certainly not E. Settling things is usually a product of duty and experience — whoever chairs the meeting and answers for the result is the one more likely to call it.

Caring for someone is a skill either type can develop. ENTJ’s Fi and ESFJ’s Fe do not predict what either person will do in a particular relationship.

Bringing a spreadsheet is not a Thinking indicator. Either type can use figures to assess a margin or to consider the effect of a decision on customers.

The fourth reads no labels overlapping as the two having nothing in common. The non-overlap is about labels, not ability; both sides can run numbers and both can look after people, and the difference is only which ground tends to be taken first.

The fifth uses who speaks first as the test. What gets said first depends on role, deadline, how much information is in the room and who else is present; the same person will choose differently in different meetings.

- J (Judging): both descriptions emphasise settling plans and decisions in the outside world. Either type can wait when the information is incomplete.
- S/N: ENTJ’s Intuition gives weight to patterns, connections and possibilities. ESFJ’s Sensing gives weight to observable details, records and direct experience.

body: The pricing, store meeting and dinner examples are fictional. They illustrate ways of using information or weighing a choice. Either person can use any of the approaches.
### ENTJ and ESFJ: pricing and the gift bundle

In this fictional review, both people compare the same three price tiers and gift options using the same costs and customer feedback. One consideration is whether each option meets an agreed margin threshold. Another is what customers get for the price and how easily staff can explain the offer. Either person can weigh both.

A price can meet the margin target while being hard to explain. An offer that customers appreciate can still cost more than the business can sustain. The fictional review illustrates the need to check both consequences before choosing.

Give both reviewers the financial assumptions and the staff feedback. Have each explain the basis for the numbers and what customers will hear. Allocate the work by access to information, experience and responsibility.

Write down what a customer might ask at each tier and what a staff member could say in response. Later, review sales, returns and repeat purchases together. Two fictional weeks of figures are not enough to establish a trend.
### ENTJ and ESFJ: a store manager objects to the price

In this fictional meeting, a manager says the product will not sell at the announced price. With the same store records, both reviewers can check what happened at comparable prices and look for a pattern that might explain the objection. Neither reaction establishes a type.

A store-level observation may reveal a problem that an aggregate figure hides. It may also reflect conditions unique to that store. The question is what evidence would support a change and where that change would apply.
The team can distinguish the evidence for changing a price from the consequences of changing the launch date. Record what is verified, what still needs checking and which choices remain open.
### ENTJ and ESFJ: twelve people for dinner on Saturday

(Fictional scene) Twelve people at home on Saturday, three of them children, one elder who does not eat spicy food. One person produces a timetable: when to shop, how many dishes, who washes up, with six o'clock fixed; the other makes calls one by one: who avoids what, who is bringing whom, whether the hard chair will do for the elder.

The two arrangements guard against different risks. The timetable guards against the day going sideways: not enough food, everyone arrived with nothing on the stove, the kitchen jammed; the calls guard against someone unable to eat, short of a seat, or placed where they cannot settle. Both risks are real, and either person can think of either one first.

The costs are plain: the timetable alone gets the food right and may leave people uncomfortable; the calls alone can reach Friday with no menu. The workable version runs both lines with a deadline each: numbers and dietary needs settled by Thursday, menu and seating by Friday. Who owns which line depends on who is at home that day and who knows these relatives better, not on type.

Either host can check dietary needs, revise the menu or prepare a schedule. In this fictional example, the hosts can compare the risks they each noticed and decide what still needs checking. The order of those checks does not identify either type.

Go back over how you read the source of information in the S/N items and the standard of judgement in the T/F items, and note which answers reflected the requirements of a post rather than your own habit.

sections.body_md:
**Framework sources**: preference definitions follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.themyersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type-dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/). These external sources explain what the preferences mean and the basic idea of type dynamics; they are not used to infer any person's behaviour.

**Four-position convention on this page**: Te–Ni–Se–Fi for ENTJ and Fe–Si–Ne–Ti for ESFJ follow the common in-site writing; the attitude of the third process is marked differently across sources, and this page takes the common version as an editorial convention, not as the Foundation's only reading, and not to infer processing order, areas of strength or collaboration outcomes.

**Editorial fiction note**: the pricing and gift bundle, the objection in the store meeting and the Saturday dinner are editorial fiction, used only to practise telling two kinds of ground apart; they correspond to no real company, store or person, and are not pricing, division-of-work or management advice.

**Scope limits**: "tends to" marks emphasis inside a model, not a statistical finding about how often anyone behaves this way; this page contains no measured data and no sample. Assessment results are not for ranking ability, hiring screens or predicting relationships, and are not for judging whether two people are suited to working or living together; matters needing professional judgement belong with practitioners qualified in them. The FermatMind assessment uses a separate item bank and scoring, and its scope is set out in the [scoring and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).
